name: Kraków
info: Kraków is a city on the Vistula in the Lesser Poland region of southern Poland, a fortified settlement from about the 8th century, the seat of Polish monarchs from 1038 to 1596 and today the second-largest city of Poland.

facts.founded: Around the 8th century, as a fortified settlement of the Vistulans, a Lechitic tribe; a legend attributes the founding to the mythical ruler Krakus.
facts.where: On the Vistula river in the Lesser Poland region of southern Poland, about 219 metres above sea level, at the meeting of the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland, the Małopolska Upland, the Sandomierz Basin and the foothills of the Carpathians.
facts.known: Wawel Hill with its castle and cathedral; the seat of the Piast and Jagiellonian kings; the Jagiellonian University of 1364; the Main Market Square and St Mary's Basilica; the Jewish quarter of Kazimierz; the Kraków Ghetto; Karol Wojtyła, who became Pope John Paul II
facts.today: Kraków is the second-largest city of Poland and the capital of the Lesser Poland Voivodeship, and its Old Town is a World Heritage Site.

t: Kraków grew from a fortified settlement of the Vistulans on Wawel Hill into the seat of the Polish government from 1038 and the capital of the kingdom until Sigismund III Vasa moved his court to Warsaw in 1596.

The city was sacked by the Mongols in 1241, rebuilt from 1257 with Magdeburg rights, and gained the university founded by Casimir III in 1364, which became a centre of Polish learning and art under the Jagiellonian kings.

After the partitions it passed to Habsburg rule, became a Polish national and cultural centre under Austrian Galicia, and was the capital of the General Government in the Second World War, when its large Jewish population was confined in a ghetto and murdered.
dyk: The so-called dragon bones displayed at the entrance of Wawel Cathedral, tied to the legend of the dragon of Wawel Hill, are most likely those of a mammoth.
ev: Vistulans found a fortified settlement on Wawel Hill

sections.origins:
Kraków stands on the Vistula in the southern part of Poland, about 219 metres above sea level, where several physiographic regions meet: the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland in the north-west, the Małopolska Upland in the north-east, the Sandomierz Basin in the east and the Western Beskidian Foothills of the Carpathians in the south. The earliest evidence of human settlement comes from the Stone Age, on the site of Wawel Castle. The city began as a fortified settlement of the Vistulans, a Lechitic tribe, around the 8th century.

A legend attributes the founding to the mythical ruler Krakus, who built the town above a cave occupied by a dragon, Smok Wawelski. Many knights failed to drive the dragon out, but Krakus fed it a poisoned lamb, which killed it. The name is traditionally derived from Krakus, a ruler of the Vistulans; its true origin is highly disputed among historians, and it may come from the word kruk, meaning crow or raven. Krakus is first recorded, as Grakch, in 1190.

Before the Polish state formed, Kraków was the capital of the Vistulans. They were subjugated for a short period by Great Moravia, and the city then passed to Bohemia, which held it until the Piast ruler Mieszko I took it towards the end of his reign.
sections.growth:
By the end of the 10th century Kraków was a leading centre of trade. Brick buildings went up, among them the Royal Wawel Castle with the rotunda of St Felix and Adauctus, Romanesque churches such as St Andrew's, a cathedral and a basilica. Its population doubled from 5,000 to 10,000 between 1100 and 1300 and stood at 14,000 in 1400, and by 1550 the metropolitan area had 18,000 inhabitants.

In 1257 the city was rebuilt after the Mongol attacks on a new location act, and Bolesław V the Chaste gave it city rights modelled on the Magdeburg rights, with tax benefits and new trade privileges. Medieval Kraków was surrounded by a defensive wall of about 3 km with 46 towers and seven main entrances, built over two centuries. In 1335 Casimir III the Great declared two western suburbs a new city, Kazimierz, and in 1364 he founded the university.

The city continued to grow under the Jagiellonian dynasty. As the capital of the Kingdom of Poland and a member of the Hanseatic League it drew craftsmen, businesses and guilds from abroad. The Renaissance reached it in the late 15th century with Italian artists. Veit Stoss finished the high altar of St Mary's Church in 1489, and under Sigismund I the Old the Wawel Castle was remade as a Renaissance palace.
sections.rulers:
Kraków was the seat of the Vistulans, then briefly held by Great Moravia, and a Bohemian duke, Boleslaus I, took it in 955. Mieszko I, the first acclaimed ruler of Poland, took it from the Bohemians and added it to the Piast holdings. In 1038 it became the seat of the Polish government. The Testament of Bolesław III Wrymouth, which took effect in 1138, divided Poland into five provinces and named Kraków the Seniorate Province, to be ruled by the eldest male of the royal family as High Duke. Infighting among his descendants followed, and the fragmentation of Poland lasted until 1320.

The Jagiellonian dynasty reigned from 1386 to 1572. When Sigismund II Augustus, the last of the Jagiellons, died childless in 1572, the throne passed to Henry III of France and then to other foreign-based rulers in quick succession, and the city's importance declined. In 1596 Sigismund III Vasa moved the administrative capital of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth to Warsaw.

After the partitions Kraków fell to the Habsburgs. Napoleon made it part of the Duchy of Warsaw in 1809, and the Congress of Vienna in 1815 created the Free City of Cracow. After the uprising of 1846 it was annexed to the Austrian Empire as the Grand Duchy of Kraków, within Austrian Galicia. Austrian rule ended in 1918, and Kraków joined the Second Polish Republic.
sections.life:
The city's population was mixed from an early date. By the end of the 13th century German-speaking burghers formed the majority of its magistrates and merchants. After the rebellion of the wójt Albert in 1311, in which many of them were massacred or fled, the burgher class was gradually re-Polonised. The city's law, with the guilds' depictions and descriptions, was recorded in German in the Balthasar Behem Codex. A cathedral school had existed since 1150, and after 1364 the royal chancery and the university brought a first flowering of Polish literary culture. Nicolaus Copernicus studied at the Academy, and Johann Haller had a printing press in the city by 1500.

Jews lived in Kraków from the early 12th century. In 1495 King John I Albert expelled them from within the city walls, and they moved to Kazimierz, where in 1553 the Jewish community received a licence to build its own interior walls. Synagogues such as the Old Synagogue were built there. Between the wars Kraków was an important centre for Polish Jews, with Zionist and Bundist groups and Orthodox, Hasidic and Reform Judaism side by side. In the census of 1931, 78.1% of the city's people declared Polish as their primary language and 20.9% Yiddish or Hebrew.

The Main Market Square, the largest medieval market square in Europe, lies at the centre of the Old Town. A trumpet call is sounded every hour from St Mary's Basilica and breaks off in mid-tune; according to legend it recalls a guard shot by a Mongol archer.
sections.crises:
The Mongols sacked and burned Kraków in 1241, and it was almost entirely destroyed. They ravaged it again in 1259, and a third attack in 1287 was repelled in part thanks to the new fortifications. A fire in 1494 was followed by a wave of anti-Jewish attacks. In the Swedish invasion the city was besieged and captured in 1655, and in December 1656 the Transylvanian prince George II Rákóczi, an ally of the Swedish king, occupied it. An outbreak of bubonic plague in 1707 left 20,000 of its residents dead.

In 1794 the Prussian army took the city and looted the royal treasure kept at Wawel Castle; the regalia, valued at 525,259 thalers, were secretly melted down in March 1809. The Kraków Uprising of 1846 was crushed by the Austrian authorities, and in 1850 a large fire destroyed about 10% of the city.

In the Second World War, in November 1939, the Germans arrested more than 180 university professors and academics and sent them to the Sachsenhausen and Dachau concentration camps; the survivors were released after protests. In March 1941 the Germans designated the suburb of Podgórze as the Kraków Ghetto, where many Jews died of illness or starvation. The largest deportations came from June to September 1942, with mass deportation from the ghetto in the first week of June, and inhabitants were sent to Bełżec, Auschwitz and the Płaszów camp. About 56,000 Jews had lived in the city before the war, almost a quarter of its population of about 250,000. After the war about 5,900 remained. The city was looted but remained relatively undamaged.
sections.legacy:
The Old Town and the historic centre of Kraków, with the Wawel Castle and Cathedral, the Main Market Square, the Cloth Hall, St Florian's Gate and the Barbican and Kazimierz, were placed on the first list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1978. Wawel Cathedral holds the burials of many Polish kings. St Mary's Basilica has the altarpiece by Veit Stoss, the largest Gothic altarpiece in the world. The Planty Park, laid out between 1822 and 1830, took the place of the old city walls. The Jagiellonian University, founded in 1364, is the oldest university in Poland, and the Jagiellonian Library holds more than four million volumes, among them Copernicus's De Revolutionibus.

Under Austrian rule after 1866 Kraków became a Polish national symbol and a centre of culture and art, known as the Polish Athens. Painters and writers such as Jan Matejko and Stanisław Wyspiański lived there. After the Second World War the Polish People's Republic built the country's largest steel mill in the new suburb of Nowa Huta, which turned Kraków from a university city into an industrial centre. Karol Wojtyła, archbishop of Kraków from 1964 to 1978, was elevated to the papacy as John Paul II on 16 October 1978, the first non-Italian pope in 455 years.

Kraków is today the second-largest city of Poland and the capital of the Lesser Poland Voivodeship, with about 816,000 people.

summary: Kraków, on the Vistula in southern Poland, began as a fortified settlement around the 8th century and was the seat of Polish monarchs from 1038 until the court moved to Warsaw in 1596. It kept its university and cultural life under Habsburg rule and survived the Second World War largely undamaged.
notes: START: the city's own article says the city began around the 8th century; the history article says the earliest known settlement on Wawel Hill dates to the 4th century and that the city dates back to the 7th century (the city article also says the town existed by the seventh century). I used c. 700 with circa true, gave only the 8th century, and left the 4th and 7th century claims out.
FIRST RECORD: the city article gives 965 (and Moravian rule 876-879, Boleslaus I capture 955); the history article gives 966. I left the first written record out.
CAPITAL FROM 1038: the city article and the lead of the history article say 1038; a later sentence of the history article says Casimir I made Kraków the seat 'sometime after 1042'. I used 1038.
GENERAL GOVERNMENT: the city article says Kraków became its capital on 26 October 1939; the history article says 4 November. I gave only 1939.

GHETTO END: the city article says the ghetto was liquidated in March 1943 and also that the last Jews were deported by September 1943; I left the end date out. The 1942 deportations are as the article gives them.

Sonderaktion Krakau: 'more than 180' (city article) and 184 (history article, 6 November); I used the former. The city article gives Poland's population of Jews in Kraków as 56,000 before the war rising to about 70,000 by November 1939; another passage gives 60,000-80,000 of 237,000; I kept the first figures. A different passage gives 'at least 90 synagogues' and another 120 in the 1930s; both left out.

Population 1550: the city article says 18,000 for 'metropolitan Kraków' and a fall to 15,000 in the next fifty years, then 28,000 in the early 17th century; I gave only the 1550 figure. The present population is the article's 816,614 rounded to about 816,000.

Kingdom of Poland and the Hanseatic League, the Golden Age, and Kasper Straube's 1473 print are in the city article and were left out for space. The Austrian-era 'Polish Athens' is as both articles give it.

1794: the city article says the uprising led to the third partition and Habsburg rule; the history article says Prussia took Kraków on 15 June 1794 and that it became Austrian in 1795. I used the 1795 date for the event list and kept the Prussian capture in the crises section.
The legend of the dragon is given as the articles tell it; the trumpet legend and the Lajkonik tradition are only partly used (Lajkonik left out).

Dates beyond the articles' dating: 'Bolesław V the Chaste' is named by the city article as the duke who incorporated the city in 1257; the history article says it received Magdeburg rights 'from the king'. I followed the city article.
